# Opencode-Self-Improvement

Durable memory for [opencode](https://opencode.ai): the decisions, commands and facts an agent should still know next week, plus a one-command per-repo setup.

Say "we use Bun, not npm — npm keeps breaking the lockfile" on Monday. A session you start on Tuesday already knows it, and why. A memory that turns out wrong is superseded, never deleted, and `memory_undo` rolls it back.

Every figure here carries a marker: **measured** (read off a live store), **bench** (a deterministic synthetic workload, reproducible with the command printed under the table), or **illustrative** (sample output showing shape, not a measurement). A number without a marker is a claim that has not been checked.

## Quick start

**1. Add the plugin** to `~/.config/opencode/opencode.jsonc` (global) or a project `opencode.jsonc`:

```json
{
  "$schema": "https://opencode.ai/config.json",
  "plugins": ["opencode-self-improvement"]
}
```

**2. Restart opencode.** On the desktop app a later config edit needs `opencode service restart`: relaunching the app leaves the background service, and the options it already parsed, alive.

**3. Run `/repo-init`** in each repo you work in. It stores that repo's test / build / lint / typecheck commands as memories, so the next session does not rediscover them. Rerun `/repo-init force` after a refactor.

After that, memory is just conversation: ask the agent to remember something and it sticks.

Other install routes — `opencode plugin add`, the Bun version floor, how an unpinned entry resolves `@latest`, and pointing the entry at a checkout: [docs/reference/install.md](docs/reference/install.md).

## What you get

Think of it as a lab notebook the agent keeps for your repo, plus a librarian who checks every entry before filing it.

- **Write gates — a CI check for facts.** A memory citing `parseHeader()` in a file you deleted is refused before it is stored, not after a future session trusts it. Near-duplicates collapse, and a contradiction with a retired memory is rejected. Every refusal lands in `memory_evidence` with its reason.
- **Budgeted injection.** Relevant memories ride the prompt on their own, capped at `injectBudget` characters. The block is cache-stable: a write somewhere else in the store does not cost you a cache miss.
- **Repo scoping.** Every row carries the repo that wrote it, so project A's facts never surface in project B. A preference you want everywhere goes in with `memory_remember global: true`.
- **Nothing is deleted.** `memory_update` supersedes the old row, `memory_forget` records a retirement, `memory_undo` restores a snapshot.
- **Memory-aware compaction** — a long session hands its durable facts to the summarizer instead of losing them.
- **Safe across concurrent sessions** — a reader sees the previous store file or the new one, never half of either.
- **Decay and consolidation** — `memory_decay` retires stale open threads, `memory_consolidate` proposes near-duplicate merges. Both are dry-run-first and write nothing you did not approve.
- **Export / import (JSONL)** — back the store up or move it between machines; every imported row re-enters through the same gates. See [Export and move between machines](docs/internals/export-import.md).
- **Surfaces** — a footer badge, the `/memory` panel, `/memory-report` for chat clients, and a browser admin editor. See [docs/reference/surfaces.md](docs/reference/surfaces.md).
- **Secret redaction** — credential-shaped values become `[redacted]`. See [docs/internals/secret-redaction.md](docs/internals/secret-redaction.md).
- **`memory_*` tools** — `memory_remember`, `memory_recall`, `memory_update`, `memory_forget`, `memory_undo`, `memory_status`, `memory_evidence`, `memory_export`, `memory_import`, `memory_decay`, `memory_consolidate`, `memory_merge_review`, `memory_list`, `memory_init`.
- **Auto-capture** — at the end of a turn, and again at compaction, one cheap model pass reads what just happened and proposes facts worth keeping. They face the same write gates as anything you save by hand. On by default, and it inherits your session's model; `autoCapture: false` turns it off. See [Auto-capture](#auto-capture).

Memory is stored outside every repository, under `~/.config/opencode/memory` by default (override with `OPENCODE_MEMORY_DIR`). To start over, delete that directory.

## Options

Zero configuration is the default. Two options change what the model sees:

| Option | Default | What it does |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `injectBudget` | `1200` | Character cap on the injected relevance block and each contextual pull. |
| `frontierBudget` | `3 × injectBudget` | Character cap on the session-start open-threads block. A thread longer than the budget is not injected and is reported as omitted. |

Everything else goes in the object form of the plugin entry, and is documented once with its invalid-value rule: the capture options, `contradictionSurface`, `notifyBlocked`, the contextual pull's scope (`pullOutputChars`, `pullTools`, with the bench behind each default), and every environment variable in [docs/reference/options.md](docs/reference/options.md). Read [docs/reference/flags.md](docs/reference/flags.md) before flipping `OPENCODE_MEMORY_DEDUP`, `OPENCODE_MEMORY_SYMPTOM` or `OPENCODE_MEMORY_QUERY_GATE` — each switches off behaviour a measurement decided, and each has an invalid-value rule that surprises people.

## Auto-capture

Auto-capture is the part that notices facts on its own instead of waiting to be asked. At the end of a turn — and again at compaction, before the summarizer replaces the transcript — one cheap model pass reads what just happened and proposes up to `captureMax` candidates (default 3). They face the same four write gates as anything you save by hand, and a 5-minute cooldown per session and trigger bounds the spend.

It is **on by default** and needs no model name to run. With `captureModel` unset, each pass uses the model your session is already using, or the host default. Name `captureModel` only to pin one model: an explicit value that is not `provider/id` turns auto-capture off with a startup warning rather than substituting a model you did not choose.

**What that default means for your data.** Because the switch is on, installing this plugin sends a copy of the conversation to your configured model at every turn-end and every compaction. The copy excludes reasoning content and runs through the credential scrubber first, and anything the pass proposes still faces the same write gates as a manual save — but the read itself is real, and it goes out over your provider. Set `autoCapture: false` if you do not want that:

```json
{
  "plugins": [{ "package": "opencode-self-improvement", "options": { "autoCapture": false } }]
}
```

**The honest caveat.** The trigger fires and the write survives on a real host: `e2e/capture.test.ts` drives `opencode run` and a capture pass starts in 12 of 12 runs. What has not been seen is a live store completing a pass — no `auto_capture_*` line exists anywhere in the maintainer's evidence history — and nothing about quality is measured: what auto-capture would write, how often it duplicates a memory you would have written yourself, and what it costs. Because the switch is on by default, that unmeasured pass runs on every install unless you turn it off; `autoCapture: false` is the one-line answer if you would rather wait for the numbers.

What has been established, and by which kind of evidence, is itemised in [docs/internals/auto-capture-evidence.md](docs/internals/auto-capture-evidence.md). Read that file before quoting any figure in it — two of the entries are defects found in the measuring bench itself, and the corrected numbers are the ones recorded there. `bench/capture-trigger-results.md` is a **bench** simulation of trigger *timing* with a scripted extractor; it answers "which moment is worth mining", not "does this earn its keep".

**Am I armed?** `memory_evidence` answers on the `plugin_load` line: `capture=on` (the default), `capture=off` (`autoCapture: false`), `invalid_model`, `no_capabilities`, or `switch_mismatch`. Once armed, an empty turn leaves one of these lines: `capture_cost` a verdict, `auto_capture_skipped` nothing durable, `auto_capture_start` alone a pass cut before its verdict, `auto_capture_dispose` no turn-end event seen. On desktop this needs `opencode service restart` after an edit — relaunching the app keeps the old service and its already-parsed options alive.

## How memory is written

A memory is a claim about your code, so it gets checked like one. Four gates run before anything is stored, and each emits an ordered evidence line:

1. **GATE-1 — code references resolve.** Call signatures and paths embedded in the memory are checked against your live source tree.
2. **GATE-2 — no stale memory applies here.** References that drifted out of date are superseded or the write is blocked.
3. **GATE-3 — no duplicates.** Near-duplicates collapse into the existing row; a contradiction with a superseded memory is rejected.
4. **GATE-4 — promotion or block.** The row lands, or the call returns the reason.

Nothing is deleted. `memory_update` supersedes the old row and `memory_forget` records a retirement, so history stays readable, and `memory_undo` restores a snapshot when a change turns out wrong. `memory_update` picks its row by `query` — an id, a clock fragment such as `00:11:22.123`, or a unique substring of its text — and a query that matches nothing, or several rows, writes nothing and says so. What carries over to the new row, what a `PARTIAL` reply means for the rows on disk, and what promotion evidence samples: [docs/internals/write-gates.md](docs/internals/write-gates.md).

**Guided constants (#349 / #351, experimental).** You and the code disagree about a constant, and who is right depends on what you said: capture records whether you stated the required value (`spec` — you are the authority) or described how working code behaves (`behavior` — code is the authority), and the CONFLICT verdict follows that class. The verdict table, what the code check will read, and the accepted residual: [docs/internals/contradiction-authority.md](docs/internals/contradiction-authority.md).

## Repo scoping

Rows are stamped with your git origin (an id that survives re-clones and moves between machines) or, without an origin, a hash of the normalized directory path. Reads — injection, recall, the frontier block, compaction, `memory_forget` and decay — see the current repo plus global rows. Writes follow the stricter direction: a named session whose repository cannot be resolved has **no write target**, so `memory_remember`, `memory_update`, `memory_import` and auto-capture refuse it (evidence `write_refused`) rather than stamp your content into another workspace or publish it as an unstamped row. Preferences that should follow you everywhere go in with `memory_remember global: true`. Identity derivation and legacy hashes, evidence attribution when a session moves repositories mid-operation, and the viewer's separate admin seat: [docs/internals/repo-scoping.md](docs/internals/repo-scoping.md).

## What memory is worth, measured

Two results. Only two are quoted, each with its `n` and the seat it ran on, because the direction of an early finding flipped when the metric was corrected — see [#385](https://github.com/abogartz/opencode-self-improvement/issues/385) and [#392](https://github.com/abogartz/opencode-self-improvement/issues/392).

**The metric.** `work = session generation + capture generation`, with cache read and cache write reported separately and never folded into a total. Capture is a separate model call made after the turn, so it appears in no session's usage: a meter that reads session numbers alone reports this plugin's own cost as exactly zero. On the seat below `input` is only the **uncached remainder** — one run reported 13,393 of 187,856 tokens that actually moved, 7%.

| Result | n | Seat | What was measured |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Transport.** A fact learned in one session reaches a later session that provably cannot obtain it any other way | 5 per arm, with the empty-store floor verified first | `evo/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-UD-Q4_K_XL`, local seat behind a recording proxy | empty store **0/5** (every failure: the artifact was never written), the same store seeded **5/5**. The fixture is leak-checked: no form of the answer is in any file the agent sees, including its own documentation |
| **Reuse.** A memory reduces the work on a task the agent already passes | 6 pairs | same seat | median of the six per-pair L2/L0 work ratios — sorted 0.54, 0.79, 0.84, 0.98, 1.06, 1.23, middle two averaged — **0.91×**, higher in 2 of 6, inside the pre-registered 0.80–1.25 band: **no measurable effect at 20% resolution**. A memory about an unrelated task: **0.99×**, same estimator, higher in 3 of 6 |

**What is not claimed here.** No token saving. No dollar figure. The seat above is a local box with no cache price; on a hosted provider a cache miss costs roughly 0.1× read and 1.25× write, which is a different claim and cannot be quoted from these numbers.

**Rules for any cost claim in this repository** — the published numbers live in `bench/claims.json`, and `test/host/claims.test.ts` enforces that file and this one in CI:

- No cost claim below **n=6 pairs per arm**. A ratio at `6 ≤ n < 21` is labelled **"20% resolution"**.
- A **seat** and a **metric** are named on the same line as the number.
- The word "cheaper" does not appear without those.
- An issue or PR body making a cost claim owes the same n, seat and metric. CI reads only this file, so that half is enforced by review.
- Nothing reproduces at n=1: the same arm on the same fixture, both runs passing, differed by more than 2× in tokens.
- Cache state is reported, never assumed. Two runs that start from different cache states are not a saving.

## Token cost and caching

Injecting memory costs prompt bytes, and prompt bytes are what a provider bills against. So the plugin treats the injected block like a cached HTTP response: it is recomputed only when the content the model is actually reading changes, and until then it is delivered byte-identically and served from cache.

- **The frozen bytes are the authority, not the store fingerprint.** A row promoted elsewhere in the store that changes nothing visible costs no cache bust. A memory *you* saved in this session is already in your own transcript, so it does not bust your cache either; a correction of a row you are riding, or anything another session, the viewer or an import wrote, still lands on your next request.
- **Two concepts, not one.** A free-text prompt must share at least two distinct concepts with a memory to be injected; one- and two-word queries need only one. Identifier spellings count once: `getUserAccount`, `get_user_account`, `get-user-account` and `get.user.account` are one concept rather than four ([#409](https://github.com/abogartz/opencode-self-improvement/issues/409)).
- **Things you said outright ride first.** A row auto-capture tagged `user-guided` — "the correct sales tax rate is 8.25%" — rides ahead of the lexical picks, newest-first, at most three, inside the budget. Only auto-capture mints the tag; `memory_remember`, updates and imports strip it, because always-riding priority is a poisoning amplifier.
- **Budgets are hard, receipts are real.** The block and each pull are capped at `injectBudget` characters, the frontier at `frontierBudget`, trimmed at whole-memory boundaries. The badge shows the provider's own `tokens.cache` accounting; a host that reports nothing shows nothing. Auto-capture is the one place with no receipt at all — it is its own call after the turn — so `memory_status` prints it as `receipt=none`, an estimate.

**Bench** — on a deterministic workload the shipped policy injects **12.3% fewer characters** than the naive policy, measured over the whole memory section: bytes on a synthetic run, not tokens and not a provider bill. The four-policy table, what the invalidation counter does and does not count, what the workload cannot show, and an author-reported provider audit (input tokens only, not a total and not a saving): [docs/internals/injection-cost.md](docs/internals/injection-cost.md). Reproduce the byte workload with `bun run bench`.

## Recall quality

No vector database, no embedding model, no API key: a keyword matcher. That is a trade, and here is the price, measured against classic BM25 on a deterministic eval (store of 200, k=3 — the production injection limit). **Bench**:

| Query, vs. the stored memory | share | R@1 | R@3 | with `kw` R@1 | with `kw` R@3 |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| lexical — reuses your project's words | 46% | 98% | 98% | 98% | 98% |
| near — reworded, one overlap | 17% | 28% | 28% | 67% | 72% |
| strict — zero shared words | 37% | 0% | 0% | 26% | 26% |

"with `kw`" is the same matcher over the same store with each row's write-time keywords indexed; the only changed variable is the index.

- **Most in-project prompts are lexical** (`bun test`, "the rate limiter", "staging deploys"): 98–100% R@3, flat from store size 50 to 500.
- **A zero-overlap paraphrase is the real limit, and write time is where you answer it.** "How we deploy" will not match a session that types "ship to staging" unless you say so: `memory_remember` asks each row for 3–5 `kw` aliases — other names, other verb forms, the literal command — indexed and never rendered. Strict R@1 0% → 26%, near R@1 28% → 67%. Narrowed, not removed.
- **Exact keyword lookup.** In a long `memory_recall` query, one complete authored keyword can identify a single visible candidate. Automatic prompt injection still requires two shared concepts for long queries.
- **`memory_recall` returns 5 rows, not 20.** A live audit of 1,090 recall events found a rank-1 row used in a later tool call at 3.4x the rate of a random store row, and ranks 11–20 at 1.16x — noise. Pass `limit` for a wider sweep.

The abstain-by-design rule, the permutation control behind the `kw` numbers, and the eval's caveats — a synthetic dataset, an adversarial class mix, single-gold scoring: [docs/internals/recall-quality.md](docs/internals/recall-quality.md). Full methodology and all store sizes: `bench/recall-results.md`. Reproduce with `bun run bench:recall`.

## Write latency

A write that cites code references builds one tree index — a single recursive walk that prunes `node_modules` and VCS directories — shared by GATE-1 and GATE-2, and reads each source file at most once. **Bench** on a 5,300-file fixture: 17ms, 15ms and 20ms for 1, 3 and 5 embedded call forms, against 105ms, 136ms and 169ms for one scan per form. The shipped column is flat because the tree is walked once no matter how many references the write cites. The fixture, the table and `bun run bench:write`: [docs/internals/write-latency.md](docs/internals/write-latency.md).

## The store keeps score

The plugin keeps a use ledger — a due-date card for every row: who looked at it, when, and how it reached them. It is append-only, never ingested as a memory, and reported in `memory_status` and the `/memory` panel.

- **Use has three distinct sources** — the row rode the injected block, `memory_recall` returned it, or a grep/read pull appended it — because "the model asked" and "the harness offered" are different facts. No prompt content is stored: the ledger keeps a scan-truncated string from the *memory* side, never your message.
- **Reinforcement is a tie-break only** (`useBoost ≤ 1.0`): a recently used row wins a tie and can never outrank a real score gap.
- **`never retrieved` is stated, not acted on.** Pruning is your decision.
- **Aggregate STORE counts are machine-wide by decision (#213 B)** — they describe the store on this machine, not your slice of it. Privacy applies to the content surfaces instead: `memory_evidence` and the recent-blocked-writes list follow each reader's repository visibility (#306).

`memory_status` joins rides to later gate checks on the same turn. For example,
`used=5 clean=0 fail_after=2 unknown=2 (eviction candidate)` records five rides,
two distinct failing turns and two rides with unknown outcomes. Totals cover
the store; individual rows follow repository visibility. Check the underlying
memory before acting on a candidate. Gate failures alone cannot establish harm.

Sample `STORE` output, the credit rule and its throttle, the consolidation tie-break, and capture lag: [docs/internals/use-ledger.md](docs/internals/use-ledger.md).

## Consolidation

`memory_consolidate` finds near-duplicates and proposes merges. It writes nothing; each proposal prints the exact `memory_merge_review` call that resolves it, and resolving is supersede-not-delete.

The rule is: never merge two entries unless every question that used to find either one still finds the merged row.

- **Deterministic.** The canonical row is the survivor's prose verbatim plus the absorbed rows' aliases as keywords. No model rewrites anything.
- **Proven by recorded reads.** Every read the ledger recorded for a cluster is replayed against the merged store, and a merge is proposed only when the canonical row catches at least as many of the cluster's own reads as the best single member did alone. A cluster with no recorded reads is reported as *unmeasured* and never merged on resemblance.

**Bench** — on the eval dataset the pass takes 200 rows to 52 with **R@3 52 → 53 and R@1 52 → 50**, and store-wide injected characters 25 945c → 6 933c. Both the regression and the budget swap are bounded in CI (`test/consolidate/consolidate-bench.test.ts`).

## Secret redaction

One best-effort credential rule set (`src/secrets.ts`) replaces recognized values with `[redacted]`, and it runs at every boundary a credential could persist: the auto-capture prompt before it leaves the plugin, the write gate before content is hashed or analysed, the final write choke point used by gated writes and the viewer's edit and restore paths, and every durable audit line. Covered patterns, and the limits that matter — hex-only secrets and prose credentials it can miss, forward-only scrubbing, and the fact that deleting a row copies it rather than scrubbing it: [docs/internals/secret-redaction.md](docs/internals/secret-redaction.md).

## Export and move between machines

`memory_export` writes the store as JSONL **as its caller can read it**: from a plugin session that means your repository plus global rows. `memory_import` reads such a file back, and every imported row re-enters through the same four gates as `memory_remember` (tagged `import`, original tags preserved). Both tools are model-facing, so a path is not a privilege: it must stay inside the store, and a symbolic link cannot carry a request out of it. The reply is a tally — `promoted`, `collapsed`, `blocked`, `skipped`, `downgraded` — not a yes/no. The move step by step, the file format, the confinement limits and the quarantine screen: [docs/internals/export-import.md](docs/internals/export-import.md).

## Surfaces

Same data behind each one (`memory_status`; no model call): the terminal **footer badge** — the injected block against its budget plus the measured session prompt-cache hit rate, with the dot color telling you whether the cache is warm — the **`/memory`** session panel, **`/memory-report`** for chat clients where the terminal slots do not exist, and a loopback-only **browser editor** (`bun memory-view`). What each shows, the badge colors, and what binding the editor to a non-loopback host costs you: [docs/reference/surfaces.md](docs/reference/surfaces.md).

Every document under `docs/`, one line each with its audience and summary: [docs/README.md](docs/README.md). The accepted architecture decisions, with status and supersession: [docs/adr/README.md](docs/adr/README.md).

## Development

Nothing merges without the full gate; CI runs it as required checks (`lint`, `test`, `smoke`), and the same sequence is one command locally:

```sh
bun run gate          # typecheck + lint + unit tests + terminal smoke & BDD
bun run gate:hooks    # once per clone: run the gate on `git push`
bun run format        # apply the shared two-space TypeScript/TSX style
```

Use Bun **1.4.4** for development checks, matching CI. `bun run test` and `bun run test:e2e` run files across at most four worker processes; cases inside each file stay sequential because fixtures share environment variables and module state.

**Feature order is BDD-first.** A new feature starts by adding or fixing a scenario in `e2e/` that describes the behavior as a user would observe it — before implementation code and before unit tests. If no scenario turns red first, the feature has no observable contract. `e2e/` boots the **real opencode CLI** in a fully isolated instance against a scripted fake model — no API keys, no shared store. It needs `opencode` on `PATH` locally, or `OPENCODE_BIN`.

How the local commands map to CI job names, what the smoke suite really boots, why the published surface is decided by `package.json` `files`, and the pre-release mutation sweep with its artifact policy: [docs/internals/development.md](docs/internals/development.md) and [docs/internals/pre-release-ritual.md](docs/internals/pre-release-ritual.md).

## Layout

Two root files are shims, and both exist because OpenCode finds plugins two
different ways. **Loose plugin discovery** reads `<config>/plugins/<name>/index.ts`
and, next to it, a sibling `tui.ts` — so the repository root carries `index.ts`
(re-exporting `src/index.ts`) and `tui.ts` (re-exporting the default of
`src/tui/panel.tsx`). **Package installs** resolve through `package.json`
`exports` instead: `"."` → `./index.ts` and `"./tui"` → `./src/tui/panel.tsx`.
Real code lives under `src/`, one directory per module. Loose discovery installs
nothing, so run `bun install` inside the copied directory: the plugin has runtime
dependencies, and one that cannot be resolved fails the load with an error about
the default export rather than the missing package
([#464](https://github.com/abogartz/opencode-self-improvement/issues/464)).

# ADR 0001 — Two-concept admission for the recall tool

Status: accepted (2026-11). Code: `src/recall/gate.ts`. Flag: `OPENCODE_MEMORY_QUERY_GATE`.

## Decision

A `memory_recall` query of three or more concepts must share two whole-word concepts with a row for that row to be returned. Shorter queries keep the permissive one-concept admission. ON by default; off only for an explicit negative value.

## Why

The tool scored rows by counting query words appearing as substrings and returned anything above zero. Measured on 404 real recall queries from 30 days of session transcripts, relevance labelled by two independent readers against a pinned store snapshot: a large share of returned rows was judged irrelevant rather than answering. The injection path already refused single-concept matches for deliberate searches; the two paths disagreeing was the bug.

## History

- The first implementation reused the tool's own substring test. It was satisfiable by accidents: `on` occurs inside `context` and `decision`, `pr` inside `preference`, `283` inside `build2837` — the motivating query `watermark 283 287 head` still admitted the row it was meant to refuse. The numbers measured with substring counting are void; do not quote them.
- Default-ON was decided with the rule: a quality fix that nobody flips on is not a fix. The off-list is explicit negatives (`off`, `no`, `n`, `false`, any zero); unset, empty, or a typo means ON.
- Admission vocabulary carries the scorer tokenizer's identifier granularity plus the underscore- and dot-joined whole forms, so prose queries find identifiers written in any style (`discount tiers` finds `DISCOUNT_TIERS`; `discount` finds `discountTiers`; `db_id` finds `table.db_id`). This closed three reproduced regressions in review; each is pinned by a composed-handler test.
- Evidence: 404-query case bank (data deliberately never committed; only aggregates were published). See issues #409 and #418 and PR #426 for the measured tables.

# ADR 0002 — Near-duplicate suppression inside the recall window

Status: accepted (2026-11). Code: `src/recall/dedupe.ts`. Flag: `OPENCODE_MEMORY_DEDUP`.

## Decision

One deterministic pass after ranking: skip a candidate whose content-token Jaccard against an already-kept row of the same scope reaches the threshold (default 0.8, ON). The newest copy of a clash takes the slot.

## Why

The live store carries repeated rows — superseded snapshots, cursor rows differing only by a timestamp, the same decision restated after a compaction — and the matcher scores them alike. With a fixed window they crowd out distinct facts, which breaks composition: two memories a later task needs together rarely fit side by side because the first one's copies take the slots. Recency decides because the duplicates are stale by construction.

## History

- Threshold guidance from the live replay: 0.5–0.7 suppresses rows that are merely related (92% of them at 0.5) and forces the window deep into the ranking; 0.8 suppresses only near-identical copies. Values below 0.5 are a misconfiguration, not an aggressive setting — at Jaccard 1e-9 a single shared fragment suppressed rows.
- The first version made four mistakes, each now pinned by a test:
  1. It scored `type` and `scope` as tokens, so same-scope rows shared two free tokens and short rows looked like copies of each other.
  2. It compared whole token sets, so a prohibition read as a copy of the permission it denies: "force push main" inside "never force push main" reaches Jaccard 0.833 and the wrong copy survived.
  3. It had no floor. Non-Latin prose tokenises to nothing under `words()`, so two unrelated Chinese rows in one scope both reduced to the empty set; the pre-floor version scored them on type and scope alone at 1.0 and deleted the second row.
  4. It treated differing numeric facts as duplicates: short tokens are dropped, so "DB 3" and "DB 4" share identical token sets and the older row was suppressed even at threshold 1.
- Default-ON followed the same rule as ADR 0001: a quality fix behind an opt-in flag is not a fix.
- Evidence: live-store replay published in the #409 record (§17) and PR #426. The replay's off-arm must set `OPENCODE_MEMORY_DEDUP=0` explicitly — with default-ON, an unset arm measures nothing.
- Re-measured 2026-11-19 over the window a repository actually reads — its own rows plus rows carrying no repository stamp (`bun bench/runners/dedup-live-replay.ts`; written up in the [live dedup replay](https://github.com/abogartz/opencode-self-improvement/blob/main/bench/dedup-live-results.md), whose counts are a dated snapshot because the store drifts). The scan neither confirms nor refutes 0.8: among the repository's own active rows no pair reaches the threshold, and once superseded history is included every candidate has a superseded side. It found two other things, and they are the useful part. Near-identical rows can stay active together: the write gate's duplicate check is exact and keyed by type, while this pass compares across types, so identical prose filed as two types lands twice and stays active. This pass is therefore not redundant with the gate. And the pass is inert on the repository's own rows because of its guards, not because the store is clean: of the pairs the pre-`fc59b84` rule would have suppressed, the dropped-chunk guard stops nearly all and the content floor the rest.
- Known limitation, from that same replay: 0.8 suppresses a pair that is not a copy. Two active rows naming two different build commands in one scope score 0.824 and pass every guard. Ranking favors recency and the pass keeps the first-ranked row of a clash, so the survivor is the newer, narrower command and the plain build command is what disappears from the reader's view. The threshold trades that against crowding; where a scope holds parallel short facts, it costs real information.
- Raising the default was evaluated on 2026-11-19 and rejected. The pair worth releasing scores 0.8235; the changed-fact pair pinned in `test/recall/dedupe-tool.test.ts` — the same runbook sentence with `friday` replaced by `monday` — scores 0.8333. Any threshold separating them must sit in a window one hundredth wide, which is a constant fitted to two observations, and 0.9 releases both and removes the recency rule above. The two rows have the same shape: one sentence, one long token swapped out. Whether that swap replaced a fact or added one is not visible in a token overlap, so this is not a threshold problem.
- The dropped-chunk guard, not the threshold, decides what this pass ever sees. Two rows differing by a timestamp have different dropped fragments and are never compared, so the cursor rows this record names as the motivation are exempt, while prose carrying no short fragments at all is compared and can be suppressed on shape alone.


## Addition groups

A clash is not always a copy. `classifyPair` reads the leftover token sets and splits three cases:
`identical` (nothing left over — one row typed twice), `addition` (one side wholly contained — the
rows name different things, so both hold), `substitution` (a leftover on each side). Only `addition`
is decidable from containment, and only `addition` keeps both rows; it takes an extra slot and the
handler marks the pair with `AMBIGUOUS` rather than deciding silently. Flag:
`OPENCODE_MEMORY_AMBIGUOUS`, on by default.

`substitution` is an interpretation, not a decision, and its absence of containment is not evidence
of a correction. Two instructions naming two scripts that both exist — `bun run bench:recall` and
`bun run bench:write` — leave a leftover on each side, score 0.882, and the older is dropped. That
predates the split and the split does not fix it: the pass has no way to learn from a row's text that
both scripts are real. It is the remaining limitation of the rule, and the reason the group marker
exists at all — where the classifier can see both readings are possible, it says so instead of
choosing.

# ADR 0003 — Identifier-aware tokenizer at two granularities

Status: accepted (2026-11). Code: `words()` in `src/recall/score.ts`.

## Decision

Each identifier (a maximal run of letters, digits, `_`, `.`, `-`, `/`) emits two granularities: the whole identifier lower-cased, and its segments split at camelCase boundaries and separators. The scan is one linear pass with no backtracking.

## Why

The shipped tokenizer kept `_` inside a token and never touched case, so `getUserAccount`, `get_user_account` and `get-user-account` were three unrelated tokens. Segments make identifier styles match each other: a query typed `getUserAccount` shares `get`, `user`, `account` with a row written `get_user_account`.

The whole form is not redundant: it preserves the exact match the shipped tokenizer had — `db_id` and `OPENCODE_MEMORY_DIR` stay single tokens, and an authored keyword stored fused (`memoryrecallthreshold`) still matches the query that cites it.

## History

- The first version of this change dropped the whole form. It abstained on `db_id` queries and broke the vocabulary bridge for camelCase aliases (#40). Both granularities are load-bearing; the regression tests say so.
- Measured on the bench fixture at the shipped configuration (`kw` indexed, store 200 and 48): lexical R@1 stays 98% and top-1 noise stays 6%. The fixture's queries never spell the same identifier two ways, so this is a correctness fix the fixture cannot price, not a measured win. The no-keyword arm moves (R@1 98% → 100%), but production indexes keywords.
- Admission (ADR 0001) reuses this tokenizer plus the underscore/dot-joined whole forms; it must never be narrower than the scorer.

# ADR 0004 — Viewer startup token on non-loopback binds

Status: accepted (2026-11). Code: `src/viewer/server.ts`.

## Decision

A non-loopback bind or allowed host mints a startup token (0600, in the store root); every request must present it. Loopback stays open. The Host/Origin layer remains as the CSRF defence it always was, but it is not the only thing between the LAN and the store.

## Why

Exposure without authentication was the defect: with a non-loopback bind every read and mutation was open HTTP for the whole LAN.

## History

- Concurrent first starts (same process or separate processes) must agree on ONE token. The claim is an atomic hard-link of a fully-written 0600 temp: `link(2)` refuses an existing target, so exactly one starter's content lands and every loser reads back the winner's complete token.
- The hard-link claim solves an ABSENT file, not a CORRUPT one. Two starters that both read the same corrupt winner used to replace it unconditionally — disagreeing on Linux, throwing EPERM on Windows. Recovery is now serialized twice over: within one process every mint runs through a promise chain, so the second starter re-reads the repaired file instead of racing the repair; across processes an `O_EXCL` lock file elects one repairman and the others adopt its token. A replacement is never unconditional.
- The reuse path enforces the 0600 contract too: `preparePrivateFile` tightens an existing file to owner-only (keeping owner bits, refusing a final-component symlink), so a token file left world-readable is repaired before it is accepted.
- The repair takes the STORE's lock. It used to take its own `O_EXCL` `.recover` file — the same shape as the #407 defect: lock state lived in a directory entry, and on Windows that entry outlives the holder whenever a third-party handle is open without `FILE_SHARE_DELETE`. An age-based steal could not rescue that case either, because the steal is itself an unlink and the same refusal applies — a viewer that hit it could never start again.
- The cookie is read WITHOUT `decodeURIComponent`: the value is a fixed-hex token we mint and set verbatim, and decoding junk like `osi-viewer=%` throws `URIError` on the auth path — a 500 where a malformed credential must simply be refused. The raw value cannot match, so it falls through to 401.
- A stale cookie from before a supported rotation is refused as one (F2): the token file is the single truth.
- Evidence: the review thread on issue #223.

# ADR 0005 — Two-phase teardown for capture passes

Status: accepted (2026-11). Code: `src/capture/runtime.ts` (`PassPhase`, `DRAIN_LIMIT_MS`).

## Decision

A capture pass records the instant `generate.text` resolves (`pastModel`). Teardown treats the two phases differently:

- A pass PARKED in `generate.text` when the host disposes must never write — the caller may remove the store the moment cleanup resolves.
- A pass that already HOLDS its model answer drains, bounded by `DRAIN_LIMIT_MS` (1000 ms): the answer exists, the gate is milliseconds of local work.

## Why

One disposal signal conflated the two situations and the conflation killed the feature on the CLI. Aborting past-model passes is why most real `opencode run` passes recorded `capture_cost` and no row — 9 of 12 in one sample, 6 of 12 in a controlled A/B. The abort fired on the healthy path, in the only window capture is allowed to run. Past-model passes are bounded by the drain instead, which is what the drain is for.

## Related

- Passes in flight are tracked so teardown can stop them; a disposed-during-model-answer path drops the pass rather than writing into a store the caller may be removing.
- Reads that are awaited (known-rows list, transcript) are hoisted BEFORE the model call so the disposal check runs before them: each awaited read is its own window into a teardown.
- Evidence: issues #211 and #404.

# ADR 0006 — Capture prompt integrity: redaction order and faithful citation

Status: accepted (2026-11). Code: `src/capture/runtime.ts`, `buildCapturePrompt`.

## Decisions

1. Redact the COMPLETE transcript, THEN apply the character budget. Cropping first can start the window INSIDE a credential: a PEM body whose BEGIN marker fell off, or a token whose prefix fell off, matches no pattern, and the prompt builder's own scrub (kept, defense in depth) cannot recognize a fragment.
2. Ledger failure entries are redacted AT CONSTRUCTION. Ledger args are raw tool input: a failing `bun test --token=sk-...` put the credential verbatim into the ATTESTED FAILURES block — the transcript scrub does not cover this input. Redacting at construction makes the prompt render the safe string AND the citation check compare against the same representation the model was shown.
3. A lesson citation must copy a COMPLETE displayed field. Substring presence cannot establish that a cited command ran: `includes("tsc")` accepted a lesson citing `tsc` when the only failure was `bun test --test-name-pattern tsc`. The list renders `cmd — arg`; membership is tested against each whole entry, its cmd, and its arg — never a fragment. The cmd-only citation the prompt's own example uses still passes.
4. The mined transcript is partitioned so the user's brief is labelled as the brief instead of blending into the evidence; the single un-partitioned block is the fallback when the work lines alone are too thin (a seeded transcript with no message array behind it), which keeps the old prompt shape rather than silently dropping the prose.
5. The user's turns are decoded from the message array rather than read back out of rendered text. Everything that vouches for "these are the user's own words" goes through that decode.

## Evidence

Review findings on issues #384 and #364; the credential-cropping window from #132.

# ADR 0007 — Symptom-first opening for learning and blocker rows

Status: accepted (2026-11). Code: GATE-3 region of `src/gate/gate.ts` (`symptomRuleEnabled`). Flag: `OPENCODE_MEMORY_SYMPTOM`.

## Decision

A `learning` or `blocker` row must open with the observable trigger a future session will hit: `When <symptom>: ...`. ON by default; `OPENCODE_MEMORY_SYMPTOM=off` is the escape hatch for automation holding a pre-0.28 backlog.

## Why

The measured gap is the whole argument: the same lesson surfaced 0/8 written as a session diary and ranked 1-7 written symptom-first, because the future searcher is typing the symptom, not the lesson.

## Consequences

- The backlog is repairable (`scripts/symptom-fixer.ts`); silence is not.
- New-vs-legacy distinction: a rewrite that carries the supersede target's content byte-identical is a metadata repair, not a new lesson. Retagging quarantined rows and metadata-only `memory_update` on a legacy row re-submit unchanged prose — blocking them would stall quarantine repair forever and make legacy rows uneditable. New prose against a `supersedesTs` is still a new lesson and still blocked.
- Evidence: issue #419.

# ADR 0008 — Availability verdicts tag rows; they never refuse them

Status: accepted (2026-11). Code: `src/capture/available.ts`.

## Decision

When the working tree already states a captured fact, the row is STORED and TAGGED (`available`), never dropped. Retrieval sorts tagged rows last within their score band.

## Why

Measured on this repo's live store (1,166 real captured rows): the original refusal rule rejected 30 rows and 29 of those were wrong — the note "OpenCode V2 (v2.0.26) does NOT run LSP servers" was refused because it merely contained the string `bun test`. A wrong match therefore costs a tag, not a fact. A silently dropped candidate leaves no trace to recover from.

## History

Four review rounds on the original rule found the same defect each time — text that was merely short or partly matched was read as already known — and each round patched one instance:

- Partial matching refuses new facts riding a restated fragment (a README rule + "; Finance confirmed the supplier rate is 1900"). Both rules used to refuse on one hit.
- A length cutoff dropped `Never` from `Never \`npm run deploy\`.` (cutoff 16 characters); an empty residual list was then read as proof the whole candidate was restatable. A short fragment is where a prohibition, a window or a number lives. The length test was removed; "states nothing" is the FILLER test, not a length.
- Command spans stripped after ONE declared gate was found erased undeclared prerequisites from the row before deciding.
- A bare `indexOf` matches INSIDE the opposite assertion: with `We do not use tabs for indentation.` in the README, the candidate `Use tabs for indentation.` was refused as available — the store would have held the reversal of the rule the gate had just read. A hit must begin and end on a word boundary and agree in POLARITY.
- The RESTRICTION list the design replaces tried to decide whether a candidate says anything NEW; an open vocabulary can never do that — any word left off the list reopens the class. The replacement is a whitelist for FILLER, the only direction a word list can safely go: a word left off it is read as a claim and the row is kept.

Temporal/conditional words and modals are deliberately absent from the reversal list: a manifest declares THAT a command exists, never when it may be run.

Evidence: issues #397 and #402.

# Auto-capture: what the evidence covers

Three different claims get confused constantly, so this file names them
separately: the event fires, the write survives, and a live store with a live
model completes a pass. The first two are shown. The third has never been
observed.

What has been established about auto-capture, by what kind of evidence,
and what remains unverified. The status and the arm/diagnose answer stay
in the README; this is the record behind them.

## What has been established

What is established, from tests and fixtures (no live store involved):

- **The trigger events are ones the host actually emits.** Capture subscribes to `session.execution.succeeded` and `session.execution.interrupted`, the two turn-end events present in a recording of the desktop service (`test/fixtures/host-events.jsonl`). `session.idle`, `session.status` and `session.execution.failed` are *declared* by the host but absent from that recording, so they deliberately do not trigger capture; `test/identity/event-fidelity.test.ts` refuses a trigger that is only declared. An earlier revision subscribed to `session.idle` and stayed silent for days with no signal — reading a declared event as an emitted one is the failure that fixture exists to prevent.
- **The path runs under simulated host traffic** — unit tests hand the plugin the recorded envelopes and assert a candidate lands through the write gate, including conservation (a near-duplicate collapses at the gate instead of writing a second row): `test/capture/capture-auto.test.ts`, `test/capture/capture-compaction.test.ts`. No terminal e2e scenario covers the trigger, so the simulated envelope is the strongest evidence that exists — and fabricating the envelope is exactly what passed while this feature was dead.
- **Identity triggers have their own recording check.** `test/identity/event-fidelity.test.ts` checks `IDENTITY_EVENT_TYPES` against the original 2.1.4 recording plus `test/fixtures/host-session-move.json`, a normalized one-frame extract from a separate 2.2.2 move capture. The extract must declare nonempty provenance and its retained envelopes must round-trip through the lockfile-pinned `@opencode/schema` 2.0.32 decoder. These checks reject missing metadata and malformed envelopes; they do not authenticate the capture. The identity replay uses the plugin subscription, but live plugin rebinding remains unverified. The recording version is distinct from the CI host pin (2.0.26).

- **Teardown stops work that is still in flight.** `generate.text` does not take the abort signal, so a capture parked mid-model-call used to wake up after the host disposed the plugin and run the whole write gate against a store its caller had already removed. Cleanup now aborts the subscription, every pass re-checks the signal after the model call and between candidates (a gate already mutating is never cut in half), and cleanup drains the tracked passes under a one-second bound — teardown never waits on the model. `test/capture/capture-dispose-drain.test.ts` parks a capture, disposes, releases, and asserts that no row and no evidence line carries a timestamp after disposal (#211).

# Contradiction authority: the code check and its limits

You say the retry limit has to be `5`; the code says `3`. Before the plugin
takes sides it has to be sure it is reading a real declaration, so the check is
deliberately narrow — and what it refuses to decide is the more useful half of
this document.

## Who is the authority

Capture records the kind of statement, and the verdict follows the class:

| Captured statement | Class | Verdict on a detected conflict |
| --- | --- | --- |
| User states the required value for a declared constant | `spec` | The user is the authority; change the constant to the stated requirement. |
| User describes how working code behaves | `behavior` | Code is the authority; keep the constant and raise the mismatch with the user. |
| Authority is unclear | Omit `klass` | Keep plain guidance and its staleness caveat; emit no CONFLICT verdict. |

## What the check will read

One thing: a unique top-level `const` with a literal value. Comments, string
examples, local declarations and computed expressions cannot establish an
authority verdict. The scan is bounded to 300 source files, 256 KiB per file
and depth 3, preferring `src/`, and it does not follow source links or resolve
imports.

Anything it cannot settle — an ambiguous declaration, unreadable or invalid
source, an exhausted budget, a claim outside its reach — keeps the plain
guidance and its staleness caveat and emits no verdict. The JavaScript/TypeScript
parser loads only when a row needs a code check; an explicit opt-out never
loads it. Use attribution keeps the stored row's identity and prose while
coverage counts only references present in the delivered text.

## The residual, accepted

A user-stated **wrong spec** still classifies as `spec`, and its verdict
follows that stated requirement even if it breaks the current tests. The plugin
does not infer a hidden test suite's authority and does not silently override
the user's requirement. Asking an oracle or inventing an extra authority class
is outside this contract.

Classification can also simply be wrong: a code comparison verifies a value
mismatch, not the user's intent.

Per the [maintainer's rollout decision](https://github.com/abogartz/opencode-self-improvement/pull/363#pullrequestreview-5819556342), the default is ON for full benchmarking after merge and can be revisited. The seat-model and merged-main confidence runs in #350–#352 remain outstanding; enabling the feature is not a claim that those benchmarks passed.

# Development internals

What the local commands really run, what the smoke suite boots, and how the
published npm surface is decided. The commands themselves and the BDD-first
rule stay in the README.

## Local command to CI job

| Local command | Where it runs in CI | Gates a merge |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `bun run typecheck` | inside the job named `lint` | yes, under that name |
| `bun run lint` | `lint` | yes |
| `bun run test` | `test`, re-run in `test-windows` | `test` yes; `test-windows` reports only |
| `bun run test:e2e` | `smoke` | yes |

`tsc --noEmit` has no check of its own in CI — it runs inside `lint`, so a green `lint` silently implies a green typecheck.

`bun run lint` checks lint rules and TypeScript/TSX formatting, and CI calls the same command. Lint warnings stay advisory; formatting differences fail the check. Markdown commands, prose, JSON data and historical benchmark records are outside the formatter's scope.

The test scripts run files across at most four worker processes with Bun's file isolation. To reproduce an order-dependent failure the way it would appear in one shared process, run `bun test ./test/` or `bun test ./e2e/ --timeout 240000` directly.

## What the smoke suite boots

`e2e/` boots the **real opencode CLI** against each candidate in a fully isolated instance (fresh config, fresh db, fresh memory store, empty `HOME`) driven by a scripted OpenAI-compatible fake model — no API keys. It covers loading from the source tree and from the packed npm artifact installed runtime-deps-only, plus BDD flows for remember, recall, exact and near duplicates, ungrounded claims, and forget. Needs `opencode` on `PATH` locally, or set `OPENCODE_BIN`. A `test-windows` leg also runs the suite on Windows; it reports without gating merges.

## The published surface is `package.json`

`exports` is the only import surface other code can reach (`.` → `index.ts`, `./tui` → `src/tui/panel.tsx`); `files` is the packaging list. `files` covers `src/`, so anything reachable from an `exports` target ships, but a new top-level file or directory — or anything the plugin reads at runtime outside those paths — must be added to `files` or it works from the checkout and vanishes from the npm artifact. The packed-artifact load in `e2e/` turns that miss red.

# Export, import, and moving a store between machines

`memory_export` writes the store as JSONL and `memory_import` reads such a file
back. The contract worth memorizing: **you get what you can read, and an import
is not trusted input.**

## What each tool exports

`memory_export` writes the store **as its caller can read it**: from a plugin
session that means your repository plus global rows. Full-store breadth belongs
to a session-less caller outside the plugin — the library route; the viewer has
no export route. `memory_import` reads such a file back, and every imported row
re-enters through the same four gates as `memory_remember` (tagged `import`,
original tags preserved).

## The move

```
Export my memories                              # -> <memory-root>/exports/<timestamp>-<unique>.jsonl
# …copy that file to the other machine's <memory-root>/…
Import <memory-root>/memories.jsonl             # memory_import
```

Both tools are model-facing, so a path is not a privilege: `file` must stay
inside the store — exports under `<memory-root>/exports`, imports anywhere under
`<memory-root>` — and a symbolic link cannot carry a request out of it. Pass
`scope` to export one scope. An operator running a one-off migration can restore
the old anywhere-on-disk behaviour with `OPENCODE_MEMORY_ALLOW_OUTSIDE_PATHS=1`,
which is read from the plugin process's own environment so a model cannot grant
it to itself.

## The reply is a tally, not a yes/no

| Outcome | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `promoted` | passed the gates and was stored |
| `collapsed` | near-duplicate of an existing memory; nothing written |
| `blocked` | rejected by a gate; reason in `memory_evidence` |
| `skipped` | malformed line; never reached the gates |
| `downgraded` | imported as settled because its `status:"open"` could not be vouched for |

## What the format is, and what confinement costs

The line format, what an import will believe about `status:"open"`, and the two
confinement limits no path check closes (a hard link inside `exports/`, and the
looser check on intermediate components):
[docs/internals/import-quarantine.md](import-quarantine.md).

# Import, quarantine and the viewer's edit path

A quarantined row is a spam-folder row, not a deleted one: it stays in the
store where you can read it, and is withheld from everything the model reads.

What the prose screen catches and misses, how an existing store gets
re-tagged, what releasing quarantine does, and which writes it does not
cover. The export contract and the import tally are in
[docs/internals/export-import.md](export-import.md).

Import and auto-capture also scan incoming prose for a small set of instruction-override, role-header, and download/execute patterns. Matching rows still face every write gate; a promoted match is tagged `quarantine` and withheld from recall, prompt/frontier injection, compaction anchors, contextual pull, scope/type listings, consolidation proposals, and decay. Decay previews do not quote these rows, and applied decay leaves them in the human review queue. The import reply counts quarantined promotions, gate evidence records pattern identifiers without copying the matched prose, and `/memory-report` lists review IDs for the caller's repository.

That screen only covers writes made after it shipped. A store that already holds an untagged poisoned row from an earlier `/repo-init` is repaired by the next one (#375): init scans every row the caller can read (this repository plus global) and, for each hit, writes a tagged twin through the normal gated path and retires the original — nothing is deleted, and each replacement emits its own `write_promoted` audit line. Re-running is safe: a row that already carries the tag is not touched. The reply reports `re-tagged=N`; a hit the gate refused is reported as `blocked=N` instead of passing silently, one run re-tags at most 100 rows and says how many remain, and any row GATE-2 retired along the way is named. A promoted replacement whose audit line itself fell is counted as `N without an audit line` rather than passing as a clean repair. This runs even when init skips on its stamp, because a stamped repository is the common case.

Review the full row in the memory viewer's **quarantined** filter. **Release quarantine** requires a reason, snapshots the pre-release row, and removes the quarantine flag and known scanner-reason tags; unrelated user labels such as `quarantine:custom`, repository ownership, row identity, blocklist, and supersession remain intact. Missing and already-released rows produce distinct, audited no-op outcomes. Existing prompt blocks refresh before the next delivery or status report when a row becomes quarantined or is released. Undoing a release can restore the quarantine flag.

This is a heuristic review queue, not a complete prompt-injection detector: legitimate documentation or quoted code can match. Markdown-bold role headers and download-then-`&&`-execute forms are recognized, but alternate role delimiters such as `[INST]` / `<<SYS>>`, base64-to-shell pipelines, paraphrased instructions, and indirect execution can evade it. Direct `memory_remember` and human viewer edits are explicit writes and are not automatically scanned: a session with that tool still has a prose channel, mitigated by the existing framing and provenance rather than quarantine. Those defenses still apply to released rows.

Always-ride guidance priority is reserved to auto-capture provenance. `memory_remember`, `memory_update` replacements, and JSONL imports silently remove `user-guided` (including comma-delimited tag entries) before the write gate; their field allowlists also exclude `ref`, `claim`, and `klass`. Ordinary tags and prose can still promote normally, but a portable file, even with an export header, cannot attest that the local user stated it. The capture path owns guidance metadata; this boundary protection does not authenticate a directly edited store or guarantee that a capture model classified a statement correctly. The reservation applies to guidance priority and contradiction verdicts (#342, #349).

The viewer is a trusted admin editor: its edits and deleted-entry restores do not run the model-facing grounding or deduplication gates, but they honor the same exact and near-match value rejections. Rejected edits leave the original row, snapshots and edit audit unchanged; rejected restores append nothing. The refusal names the rejection hash so you can explicitly lift it under **Rejections → un-reject** before retrying. Corrected numeric values and polarity changes retain the rejection check's existing exceptions. This check does not change whole-snapshot rollback policy.

Existing stores are not rescanned. A byte-identical import that collapses into an existing row does not retroactively tag that row. Export preserves quarantined rows and their tags to avoid data loss; an exported released row can be quarantined again when re-import promotes it on another machine.

## The file format, and what an import will believe

A header line (`{_export, version, exportedAt, count}`) followed by one JSON object per line (`{ts,type,scope,content,status,tags,issue}`), active rows only.

An open row is exempt from reference grounding, so that status is honored only for files carrying an export header — a hand-written file without one imports such rows as settled. Even with a header: an open row claiming `repo:"global"` is downgraded, and imported `repo` / `repoPath` stamps are kept only when they match the importing session's current repo — foreign stamps are dropped and the row is stamped for the importing repo. Re-running the same import in the same repo is a no-op.

## Keeping a path inside the store

Both tools are model-facing, so a path is treated as untrusted input rather than as permission. An export cannot write to `~/.gitconfig` or anywhere else outside the store, and an import cannot read outside it. Symbolic links are resolved before the check — including an `exports/` directory that is itself a link — so a link cannot carry a request out of the store. Exports are written `0600` and opened `O_NOFOLLOW` (both POSIX; on Windows the check before the write is the only guard).

The default name is `<memory-root>/exports/<timestamp>-<unique>.jsonl`, created exclusively, so two exports in the same second never replace each other's artifact.

Two limits no path check can close. A hard link planted inside `exports/` shares an inode with its target, so writing through it writes the target. And the check covers the final component more tightly than the intermediate path components, leaving a narrow window there. Both are stated rather than fixed because closing them means giving up the feature.

# Injection epochs and their measured cost

Prompt caching turns a boring question into an expensive one: how often do the
bytes in front of the model actually change? The plugin's answer is to freeze
the memory section and re-render only when the frozen bytes would genuinely
differ — the same reason you cache an HTTP response by its body rather than by
how many times the database was touched.

Every figure here is bytes on a synthetic workload: not tokens, not a bill.
The epoch mechanism, the deterministic byte workload behind the injection
claim, and a provider audit reported by its author.

- **Section-frozen injection.** The whole memory section — standing digest, open-thread frontier, relevance block — is computed once per epoch and delivered byte-identically until something the model actually needs changes. The epoch's authority is the **rendered bytes**, not the store fingerprint: a promoted row that changes nothing visible costs no cache bust.
- **A session never pays for bytes it is not riding.** A memory *you* saved in this session is a fact you already produced — it is in your own transcript — so it never busts your cache. The test is not "did the store change" but "would the frozen bytes still have been produced from the same inputs, minus the rows this session authored since": a correction, blocklisting, redaction or supersession of a row you are riding, and anything another session, the viewer or an import wrote, all still land on your next request.
- **Two-concept threshold.** A free-text prompt must share at least two distinct concepts with a memory for it to be injected; keyword-length queries (one or two words) need only one. Silence on single-word coincidences is deliberate; an explicit `memory_recall` search can admit a complete authored keyword unique among its visible candidates.
- **Identifiers split.** `getUserAccount`, `get_user_account`, `get-user-account` and `get.user.account` are one concept to the matcher rather than four, and a memory citing `src/recall/score.ts` answers a session that typed the path ([#409](https://github.com/abogartz/opencode-self-improvement/issues/409)). Measured on the published eval: aggregate recall unchanged, wrong-memory-first at the top falls 6% → 5%. Replayed over 1,091 logged recall queries through this scorer against the live store: 92.3% of top-5 sets are identical and 97.5% keep their top row.
- **User-stated guidance rides ahead of relevance.** A row auto-capture tagged `user-guided` — something you said outright, like "the correct sales tax rate is 8.25%" — rides the block ahead of the lexical picks: newest-first, at most three, and `injectBudget` still bounds the whole block (`test/inject/hint-channel.test.ts`). The channel exists because ranking cannot bridge vocabulary: a prompt about "the injected bug" shares no word with a row stating a tax rate, and the shipped matcher scored it zero ([#334](https://github.com/abogartz/opencode-self-improvement/issues/334)). `memory_recall` and the contextual pull stay query-driven — the channel changes only what rides the prompt. Because always-riding priority is a poisoning amplifier, the tag is minted by auto-capture alone: `memory_remember`, `memory_update` replacements and JSONL imports strip it, along with the contradiction fields ([#342](https://github.com/abogartz/opencode-self-improvement/issues/342), `test/gate/guidance-provenance.test.ts`).
- **The block re-scores at every user turn.** An epoch is not frozen at the first request: a later prompt re-scores, and the epoch MOVES only when the rendered bytes move — a prompt change that selects the same rows in the same order costs no cache bust ([#340](https://github.com/abogartz/opencode-self-improvement/issues/340), `test/inject/epoch.test.ts`). Order is part of those bytes on this build: the lexical picks render in score order, so a prompt that keeps the same rows and re-ranks them moves the bytes and pays the bust. Canonical render order, which removes that churn, is still open ([#388](https://github.com/abogartz/opencode-self-improvement/issues/388), [#396](https://github.com/abogartz/opencode-self-improvement/pull/396)).
- **Hard budgets.** Relevance block and each pull are capped at `injectBudget` characters, the frontier at `frontierBudget`, trimmed at whole-memory boundaries.
- **The pull is the un-cached channel.** The relevance block rides the frozen system prefix, so extra bytes there cost a cache bust; the contextual pull rides the tool result instead, which is free of the cache but also free of its discipline. That asymmetry is why its scope is measured per arm — `bench/runners/pull-precision.ts`, table and reasoning in [docs/reference/options.md](../reference/options.md) — and why widening it is a precision decision rather than a coverage one.
- **Nothing volatile on the cached prefix.** The standing digest carries no row count and no latest timestamp. Both used to ride the very front of the system prompt, so every saved memory rewrote the prefix and made the next request re-bill the whole conversation; the exact numbers now live where they are free — the footer badge, `/memory`, `memory_status`, the viewer.
- **Evidence is never injected**, and the standing system digest is two lines.
- **Measured, not claimed.** The plugin reads each turn's `tokens.cache` accounting and displays the actual hit rate next to the badge. The same receipts now carry what the session generated — `output` and `reasoning`, shown split, because on a reasoning-heavy seat the completion side is where the cost actually goes. A host that reports neither shows nothing, never a zero.
- **Auto-capture bills separately, and it is an estimate.** Capture is its own model call made after the turn, so it appears in no session's usage: read from session numbers, the plugin's own cost is exactly zero. That reading is the misleading one — auto-capture is on by default, so the call happens on installs that never set an option. The host exposes no receipt for it — `ctx.generate` has one member, `text`, resolving to `{ text }` with no `usage` — so `memory_status` reports chars/4 with `receipt=none` and the words "estimate, no provider receipt" on the line. Quote that number as an estimate or not at all. A pass disposed during teardown is not billed: its store is already gone, so the count undercounts by one call there.

**Bench** — deterministic workload (50 memories, 20 prompts, 3 mid-session store writes made *by the measured session*) through the plugin's real injection code. Every column is measured on the full memory section — the bytes a request actually sends — because prompt caching is a property of those bytes:

| Policy | Recomputes | Epochs whose bytes moved | Injected chars (20 turns) | Avg/turn | Worst section |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| A — recompute per prompt, uncapped (naive) | 20 | 19 | 60996 | 3049.8 | 3404 |
| B — block frozen on store fingerprint, digest rebuilt per turn | 4 | 3 | 55478 | 2773.9 | 2867 |
| C — section frozen on rendered bytes | 4 | 3 | 55258 | 2762.9 | 2856 |
| D — C + riding bytes (shipped) | 1 | 0 | 53500 | 2675.0 | 2675 |

The invalidation counter counts **byte-moving recomputes**: epochs whose memory-section bytes differ from the previous epoch. It is not a provider cache-miss or re-prefill count, and no status surface claims it is. All three synthetic writes change B and C's bytes; D records no change for these self-writes. Corrections, removals and writes by another session can still move D's bytes, as pinned by `test/inject/epoch.test.ts`. The workload re-scores only when the store fingerprint moves, so its 20 prompts never re-rank one shared set — D's `0` is not evidence about the same-set re-ranking above. D also injects 12.3% fewer **characters** than the naive policy, measured over the whole section — bytes on a deterministic workload, not tokens and not a provider bill. Reproduce this deterministic byte workload:

```sh
bun run bench
```

**Author-reported provider audit**, not a new measurement here, and **input tokens only** (on that provider `input` is the uncached remainder, so this is not a total and not a saving): [#346's six-turn local-seat audit](https://github.com/abogartz/opencode-self-improvement/issues/346#issuecomment-6714172764) compared `ee769ef` with frozen `29268ef`. The changed build used 2,065 additional input tokens over six turns (~344/turn), with one 3,257-input-token spike, and 94.4% cache share versus 97.5%. The block rode late in the system prompt, after a stable prefix; a byte-moving epoch did not re-bill the whole conversation. This run included two guided rows, so it does not isolate prompt rescoring from the hint channel or establish a bound for every provider. The status counter remains a byte-change count; provider receipts report actual cache reuse separately.

# Pre-release ritual: mutation sweep and artifact policy

A fire drill for the test suite: break one claimed invariant on purpose and
see whether anything notices. A mutant that no test kills is not a scandal —
it is a list of what the suite has been claiming without pinning.

What `scripts/test-sweep.ts` measures, when a person runs it, and which
benchmark artifacts stay out of git.

```sh
bun run sweep:test
```

`bun run sweep:test` (`scripts/test-sweep.ts`) audits the test suite rather than testing the plugin. Each mutant breaks exactly one claimed invariant in a detached `git worktree` of HEAD, runs the `test/` suite (unit + scenario) against that mutated tree, and reports whether the suite noticed. A mutant no test kills is an unpinned invariant: the test titles may claim coverage, but nothing died with the invariant. The clean tree is measured first and its failing tests are subtracted from every mutant run, so only new failures count as a kill and a flake never masquerades as one. Mutants are applied only to scratch worktrees beside the checkout, never to the working tree under your feet.

The output is a canonical mutation score — killed over total, with equivalent mutants and load errors excluded from the denominator — plus the survivors, the unpinned invariants. Survivors are the audit's output, not a scandal: some mutants are expected to survive and become entries on the unpinned list rather than red CI.

Run it when you want to know whether the suite still has teeth — after changing tests or coverage, or as a pre-release gate with `bun scripts/test-sweep.ts --fail-on-survivors`, which exits 4 when anything survives. Two lighter checks come first: `bun scripts/test-sweep.ts --validate` confirms every mutation pattern still lands on exactly one source site without running the suite, and `bun scripts/test-sweep.ts --selftest` plants a mutation in a trivially-tested pure function and fails unless the suite kills it — proof the instrument itself can go red.

**Pre-release ritual (decided 2026-11-04, #72):** before pushing a release commit, a human runs `--validate`, then `--selftest`, then `--fail-on-survivors`, and records the mutation score and the survivor list in `bench/mutation-sweep.md` (its own file, because `bun run bench` regenerates `bench/results.md` in full). Cadence is pre-release only, run by a person: the sweep is a full suite per mutant and never belongs in CI, where it would cost more than it informs.
