# Recall quality: what the keyword matcher gives up

A keyword matcher finds a memory when the words overlap. That is its whole
trick, and its whole weakness: "how we deploy" and "ship to staging" are the
same fact with no word in common. This file is what that costs, measured, and
what you can do about it at write time.

The headline table stays in the README. Full methodology and all store sizes:
`bench/recall-results.md`, reproduced with `bun run bench:recall`.

## Write-time keywords are the answer to paraphrase

`memory_remember` asks each row for 3–5 `kw` aliases: other names for the same
thing, other verb forms, the literal command. Keywords are indexed and never
rendered into the prompt, so they cost nothing to store and nothing to inject.

**Bench** — the same matcher over the same store, with the only changed
variable being the index:

- strict (zero shared words) R@1 0% → 26%
- near (one overlap) R@1 28% → 67%

A permutation control — every row given someone else's aliases — scores
29%/35%, so the gain is meaning rather than extra tokens. Auto-capture asks for
the same list, so these numbers are measured through the tool path rather than
through capture. The limit is narrowed, not removed.

## Abstaining is a feature

Free-text prompts that share one concept with a memory abstain rather than
force a guess. Wrong top-memory fell to 6%. The cost is silence in cases where
a lucky guess would have been right; `memory_recall` still covers them when you
ask on purpose.

### Explicit exact-keyword lookup

See the [transport lookup benchmark](https://github.com/abogartz/opencode-self-improvement/blob/main/bench/transport-lookup-results.md) for explicit recall and automatic injection on the same queries.

## Why the default window is 5 rows

A live audit joined 1,090 recall events to their session transcripts. A
returned row at rank 1 shows up in a later tool call at 3.4x the rate of a
random store row, ranks 2–3 at 2.4x, and ranks 11–20 at 1.16x — noise against a
0.129 null. The old default returned 17.7 rows per call, so most of the window
was context nobody read.

At limit 5, recall@1 and recall@3 are unchanged, precision rises 4.1% → 13.1%,
and 74% of the returned characters disappear. Every gold row the cut dropped sat
at ranks 6–20. Pass `limit` for a wider sweep ([#409](https://github.com/abogartz/opencode-self-improvement/issues/409)).

## Caveats on the eval

The dataset is synthetic — 52 memories and 105 queries about a fictional
project — its class mix is deliberately adversarial, and scoring is
single-gold. Read the numbers as a comparison between matchers on one fixed
set, not as a prediction about your repository.

# Repo scoping: identity, visibility and write refusal

Every row carries a label saying which repository wrote it. The label is
checked on the way in as well as the way out, and the two directions are not
symmetric: reading one extra project's memories is a nuisance, while writing
your private note into the wrong project is damage. So reads are permissive and
writes are strict.

The README states the rule; this is the boundary detail.

## Identity

Legacy whole-path-lowercased hashes accompanied by `repoPath` are matched to that directory (including real aliases), so a distinct case-sensitive sibling cannot inherit its memories or evidence. Remote-derived identities still share across clones. Stamps without `repoPath` retain key-only matching; their historical identity source cannot be recovered from the key alone.

## Who sees what

Injection, recall, the frontier block, compaction, `memory_forget` and decay only see the current repo plus global rows, resolved from the calling session's identity at flow entry. A session that reaches a plugin instance is bound to that instance's own workspace on first contact — in a process hosting several workspaces, one session never borrows the repository some other workspace's setup left behind. A session whose repository cannot be resolved at all sees global rows only; "unknown" is never "everything".

## Why an unresolved session cannot write

Writes follow that rule in the stricter direction. A named session with no resolved repository has **no write target**, so `memory_remember`, `memory_update`, `memory_import` and auto-capture refuse it (evidence `write_refused`) and store nothing. The alternatives were stamping your private content into whichever workspace's `setup()` ran last, or publishing it to every project as an unstamped row.

A caller that names no session at all (the viewer process, a restore, a script) keeps the process scope, and an explicit `global: true` is a deliberate owner. Preferences that should follow you everywhere go in with `memory_remember global: true`. Rows written before scoping existed are global. Upgrading changes nothing.

`memory_merge_review` applies the same rule to its inputs: a session may merge exactly the rows it may read — global rows plus its own repo's, from either seat — and a row id it merely knows is not authority to retire another repo's memory.

## Evidence attribution

Evidence lines carry the same stamp, so `memory_evidence` answers from the caller's repo plus global lines; a line a named session wrote while its repository was unresolvable is private to that session, and only an explicitly global (or predating-stamps) line reads as global.

Gate-authored evidence and its init/capture lifecycle records capture attribution at operation entry: if a session moves repositories while the operation runs, its audit lines remain in the starting repository's partition and can be read with `memory_evidence` from a session bound there. Init start/complete/skip, capture outcomes/refusals, and capture lag share that captured owner. A captured named session with no resolved repository keeps a session-private `sid` label even on lifecycle records that suppress call metadata; otherwise an unstamped line would appear global.

## The viewer

The viewer is an admin surface over every repo: it edits and restores a row with its own repo stamp, and the viewer's missing session scope never decides a row's visibility. Viewer audit attribution and cancellation of in-flight capture are separate boundaries.

# Secret redaction: what it covers and what it cannot

One best-effort credential rule set (`src/secrets.ts`) replaces recognized values
with `[redacted]`. Think of it as a metal detector at every door, not a safe: it
stops the recognized shapes, and it will never promise it saw everything.

It runs at every boundary a credential could persist, not one:

- over the auto-capture prompt before it leaves the plugin — the complete
  transcript is redacted *before* the character budget crops it, so a credential
  cut in half still matches its pattern;
- at the write gate, before content is hashed or analysed;
- again in the final write choke point used by gated writes and by the viewer's
  edit and restore paths;
- at the durable audit boundaries — every evidence line, every supersede field
  written into a retired row, and every deletion-audit reason.

So a recognized credential cannot persist in a new `evidence/` line, in a
deletion-audit `reason`, or in a supersede field written into a retired row,
whichever path carried it. It is not scrubbed from everything those paths touch —
see the limits below.

## Covered patterns

OpenAI `sk-`, GitHub `ghp_` / `gho_` / `github_pat_`, Slack `xoxb-` / `xoxp-`,
AWS `AKIA`, Google `AIza`, bearer tokens containing digits, PEM private-key
blocks, and high-entropy values assigned to names ending in `_KEY`, `_TOKEN`,
`_SECRET` or `_PASSWORD` (plus `password`).

## Limits worth knowing

- It can miss hex-only secrets, low-diversity passwords, and credentials written
  in prose without an assignment.
- The credential-shaped sweep needs 16 characters, so `password=hunter2` is
  stored exactly as written. That floor is what keeps a short ordinary value —
  a version string, an identifier carrying a digit — from being blanked wherever
  it follows a name ending in `_KEY`, `_TOKEN`, `_SECRET` or `_PASSWORD`, which
  is why it is a floor rather than a number to lower in passing.
- Credential-shaped `scope`, `tags` or `issue` metadata is rejected rather than
  silently rewritten.
- `memory_remember` still replies `Remembered` when content was redacted, so the
  stored text can differ from what was sent.
- Redaction is forward-only: existing stores are not scrubbed. `memory_export`
  scrubs credentials out of `content`, `issue`, `scope`, `tags` and `kw` as it
  serialises, so the file that leaves the machine carries `[redacted]` where a
  stored row still holds a token; the store itself is untouched, and origin
  stamps (`repo`, `repoPath`) are written as stored. The scrubber is a
  best-effort sweep over known token families and high-entropy credential-shaped
  values — an exotic credential can survive it, so an export is still a file you
  hand out deliberately.
- Deleting a row copies it, it does not scrub it. `deletions.logfmt` keeps the
  deleted row's `content`, `tags`, `kw` and `issue` exactly as the row held them
  — a restore-entry built from that line has to re-stamp and re-attach precisely
  what was there — and redacts only the `reason`. So deleting a row that predates
  redaction writes its credential into the audit. Snapshots carry whatever a
  stored row holds, for the same reason. That retention is deliberate (#292).

# Store concurrency, publication and permissions

Replacing a store file while other sessions are reading it is the whole
problem. The answer is a book swap, not a page rewrite: the writer builds the
complete new file, then swaps it in under a lock. A reader therefore sees the
old file or the new one, never a half-written record.

How a store file is replaced, what the lock covers, and what the plugin
does and does not do about permissions. The README states the user-visible
rules and links here.

Daily memory writes publish a complete replacement file under that lock, so concurrent readers see the previous or new complete file rather than a partially appended record. Appending a row therefore rewrites the day file (in addition to the existing timestamp-uniqueness read). On Windows, a reader handle that prevents replacement can make the write refuse after the replacement retry window; the previous bytes remain intact and the caller can retry once the handle closes. This publication rule applies to daily memory files, not append-only evidence, use, rejection, or audit logs; [#198](https://github.com/abogartz/opencode-self-improvement/issues/198) tracks the broader read boundary.

The lock covers one **file**, not the store directory. Two sessions writing different days of the same store therefore do not wait on each other. A directory-wide lock was tried first and lost writes: a whole-file publish waits up to two seconds on Windows for a reader to let go of the destination, and with one lock for the directory that wait stops every other writer in the store. Per file it stops only the writers of that file, which is what the publish's safety check needs. The cost is a database plus its write-ahead log per locked file; they exist only while a connection is open, and the number of open connections is bounded. A writer never holds two file locks at once, and batches that must serialize a whole read-then-supersede sequence (`memory_update`, `memory_merge_review`) take a separate named lock (`.store-batch.update-order.sqlite`), always before the file locks their steps take — so a batch never holds a file lock across its whole run.

Two unsupported placements. The write-ahead log needs mmap'd shared memory, which SQLite does not provide on network filesystems, so a memory root on SMB, NFS or a OneDrive-mounted folder is **not supported**: writes there can report a disk I/O error rather than serialise. Configure `OPENCODE_MEMORY_DIR` on local disk. And during the update that introduced this lock, a session still running the previous release honours `<date>.logfmt.lock` while an updated session honours the SQLite lock, so those two do not exclude each other until every running session has restarted.

On POSIX systems, new store directories use owner-only `0700` permissions and new files use `0600` (subject to a more restrictive umask) — including temporary replacements, snapshots, locks, status files and append-only logs. Accessing an existing store removes group/other permissions from its root, and tightens directories and files as they are written. Old descendants are not migrated recursively: a tightened root already stops other users from reaching them.

Three limits on that guarantee, stated plainly because they are privacy limits.

1. If chmod reports `EPERM`, `EROFS`, `EOPNOTSUPP` or `ENOSYS` — an immutable root, a foreign-owned root, or a mount without chmod support — reads stay available under the existing permissions, so owner-only traversal is **not** guaranteed. Fix ownership, mount support or permissions outside the plugin when that guarantee is required.
2. The modes do not revoke handles that are already open, and they do not protect copies or hard links made outside the private root.
3. On Windows the plugin changes no ACLs; privacy there depends entirely on the directory's existing ACL.

A store root that is itself a symlink is refused; configure its real directory instead. Ancestors outside the store are left as they are.

# The use ledger

A due-date card for every row: who looked at it, when, and how it reached them.
It answers one question you cannot answer any other way — is this memory
earning its place, or has nothing touched it in six months?

The ledger is `<memory-root>/hits.logfmt`: append-only, rotated at 2 MB, never
ingested as a memory, and reported in `memory_status` and the `/memory` panel.

## What it looks like

Illustrative output — shape, not a measurement:

```
STORE
  41 active · 12 superseded · 4 open · 6 scopes
  retrieved 33 rows in the last 30d; never retrieved 8 (20%) — reported, not acted on
  outcome-linked 7 rides over 3 rows: 3 clean row/turns, 2 failed row/turns (store-wide)
  1 candidate at ≥5 rides with no clean turn — best-effort counts are floors since 2026-11-01T10:00:00.000Z; correlation on the ride's own turn, reported, never acted on
  outcome writes dropped for this store by this process: 0
    2026-10-31T14:05:00.000Z used=5 clean=0 fail_after=2 unknown=2 (eviction candidate)
  24.1 KB total · 604 B per row · 1.3 rows/day (30d)
```

## What counts as use

Credit comes from three distinct sources, because "the model asked" and "the
harness offered" are different facts:

1. the row rode the injected block;
2. `memory_recall` returned it;
3. a pull appended it to a grep/glob/read result — searched against that call's
   arguments plus the first 512 characters of what the tool printed, so a row can
   be credited here for something the model had not asked about yet
   (`pullOutputChars` in [docs/reference/options.md](../reference/options.md) dials it back).

Credit is recorded only when the bytes were actually placed on the result. When a
pull computed rows and found nowhere to write them, the evidence log gets a
`pull_undelivered` line instead — a host that changes its result shape should show
up as a failure, not as a quieter ledger.

The writer throttles identical sets of retrieved rows to one successful line
per session and source per hour. A row can appear in multiple sets.

**No prompt content is stored.** The ledger keeps a scan-truncated string from
the *memory* side, never your message.

## What happens after retrieval

Each `memory_used` line records the turn number and turn key when available.
Each classified gate check appends a separate `ev=gate_outcome` line with
the session, turn, key, timestamp, command family and `outcome=clean|fail`.
The chat report aggregates those observations on read. On each row, `used`
counts recorded rides. `clean` and `fail_after` count distinct turns with
a classified gate after a ride. A later failure takes precedence over passes.
`unknown` counts rides without a usable later gate on that turn, including
legacy rides without a turn key when no compatible outcome exists.
Multiple rides on one turn can therefore contribute one measured turn.

The ledger drops old lines at rotation and can miss writes under contention.
The counts describe the retained observations. The dropped-outcome counter
covers failed writes in the reporting process for this store. It resets on
restart and excludes failures in other processes. A zero cannot establish
complete history.

A row becomes an eviction candidate after five recorded rides if at least
one ride has a measured outcome and none has a clean turn. A subsequent
failure can be unrelated to the row. Inspect the row and its use before
deciding whether to retire it. The report makes no store changes.

## What use is allowed to do

Reinforcement is a tie-break only (`useBoost ≤ 1.0`): a recently used row wins a
tie and can never outrank a real score gap. In consolidation, the most recently
used member of a cluster is never the merge loser.

`never retrieved` is stated, not acted on. Pruning is your decision, and retired
rows cannot inherit reinforcement: ledger rows are verified against the store on
read.

## Whose numbers these are

Aggregate STORE counts are machine-wide by decision (#213 B): they count every
repository's rows in the shared store on this machine, never just the reading
session's repository. The numbers describe the store, not your slice of it.

Outcome totals and candidate counts also cover every repository. The chat report
shows up to 20 reader-visible row IDs, prioritizing candidates. The omitted
count covers additional visible rows.

Privacy applies to the content surfaces instead. `memory_evidence` and the
recent-blocked-writes list in `memory_status` and `/memory` follow each reader's
repository visibility (#306).

## Capture lag

Capture lag is how stale the newest message was when auto-capture fired. The
line prints only when at least one `capture_lag` sample exists, which needs
auto-capture to have fired.

# Write gates and promotion evidence

A memory is a claim about your code, so it is checked the way a pull request
is: does the reference resolve, is something already on file stale, is it a
duplicate, and does it land or come back with a reason. The four gates and the
undo contract stay in the README. This file is what the audit trail keeps, and
what an update carries with it.

## What promotion evidence samples

Promotion evidence keeps a bounded sample of call IDs: the ten most recent code-engagement calls, plus the latest gate check, the latest recorded gate FAIL/fix/PASS recovery, and the latest recorded tool FAIL/PASS retry (at most 16 distinct IDs). `evidence_refs_count` is the total number of recorded session calls before sampling, including non-code tools; the sampled IDs are audit pointers, not a complete history. Grounding and memory attribution still use the full in-memory ledger. Existing evidence day-files are left unchanged: this upgrade does not backfill, compact, or delete historical audit records.

## When a cited path stops existing

A settled claim about code must point at a file the repository has, so a write naming a missing path is refused with `ref_path_missing`. That check runs on writes only. A row that was correct when it was saved goes stale on its own the moment a later refactor moves the file, and nothing notices: recall keeps quoting a path the reader cannot open.

For a retired file, write the history lookup as a single backticked command, for example `git log -- bench/runners/append-cost-198.ts`. The gate verifies every such path against file names in the checkout’s available Git history from HEAD. A missing path or unavailable history refuses a settled write. Use the exact inline spelling shown above. A plain citation of the same path still needs a file in the current tree, and the repair report lists unverified pointers for a human. The command contributes no evidence that the file exists now. The usual grounding rules still apply.

`scripts/ref-fixer.ts` repairs the mechanical cases. The default is a dry run; `--apply` writes through the same gated update path as `memory_update`, so the old row is superseded rather than edited and `memory_undo` stays the recovery path. It repoints a path under two rules, and each is narrow for a specific reason:

1. **A scored rename.** Git records a rename scored at least `R90` whose chain ends at a file that exists today and whose basename is unchanged. The floor is measured rather than guessed: this repository's renames cluster at `R090`..`R100` — the domain restructure, where the only content change is the import lines inside the moved file — and the outliers below it (`R058`, `R072`, `R080`, `R086`, `R088`) are files git scored as renames after much of their content was rewritten. The basename matters because it is what a query matches on — `src/lock.ts` to `src/store/lock.ts` still says "lock", so the row stays findable by the words that found it before.
2. **A loose citation.** The path never existed anywhere in git history and exactly one tracked file ends with it: `gate/gate.ts` for `src/gate/gate.ts`. Both halves are load-bearing. Without the history check, a path the gate once refused as hallucinated would be handed a verified reference; without the single-candidate check, the fixer would pick a directory on the row's behalf.

Anything else is reported, never rewritten. A path occupied by more than one generation — moved away and recreated at the same path, in either order around the move — is one of those: rows written against each generation cite the same string and describe different files, and nothing in a row's text says which generation it belongs to. None of that is visible in a rename count. A file moved away, recreated and later deleted leaves no second rename record; a file deleted, recreated and then moved has the rename as its newest touch. Both are one path with two creations, so the check counts how many times history created each path — an add, or a rename or copy landing on it — and refuses above one. The count applies to every path the chain walks, destination included: move `src/lock.ts` to `legacy/lock.ts`, delete it, and commit something unrelated at `legacy/lock.ts`, and the chain ends on a file the original component never occupied. The report names whichever path is ambiguous, which need not be the one the row cites. A rename that also renamed the file (`src/logfmt.ts` to `src/core/logfmt/publish.ts`) changes what the sentence asserts, and a path that once existed and is gone was retired on purpose — a row about it is the record that it existed, and rewording that is a decision, not a repair.

The edit itself is span-based, not a substring replace. Only the references `checkablePathRefs` reports are touched, at the offsets they occupy. That is the safety property: a replace over the whole string also hits a ref nested inside a longer one (`gate/gate.ts` inside `src/gate/gate.ts` becomes `src/src/gate/gate.ts`) and rewrites absolute paths that the checker deliberately skips — so the gate could never refuse the damage, because it never sees those.

Two limits worth knowing before trusting a clean report. Rows are selected by repository key, defaulting to the current directory: rows stamped for another repository, and rows with no stamp at all, are never scanned, because no tree here owns their paths. And a repointed row can still be refused, with a reason that is informative rather than a bug — the row cites a second path the rules will not touch, or it is a `learning` or `blocker` row where a content change brings the symptom-first rule into play. Both are no-ops, listed with their reason, and a run with refusals exits non-zero so a scripted caller cannot read them as success.

## What an update carries forward

`memory_update` picks its row by `query`: the row's id, a clock fragment such as `00:11:22.123`, or a unique substring of its text. Omit it and the newest entry of that scope and type is the target. A query that matches nothing, or that matches several rows, writes nothing and says so — an ambiguous selector is never resolved by picking one.

A prose edit carries the previous row's ordinary tags, issue link, retrieval keywords, open/settled standing and repository forward to the new row, so updating a `global` row from one machine keeps it global for every other. Capture-only guidance provenance is stripped by the replacement: an ordinary edit cannot re-mint a `user-guided` tag or a contradiction verdict.

Naming a row that an earlier update already superseded reports the duplicate when the live successor already holds exactly that content. When only the metadata you named differs, the update runs against the successor instead of dead-ending.

If a failure happens after the new row is already durable, the reply says `PARTIAL`. The message names what failed, the replacement stands on disk, and `memory_undo` (merge or force) brings the old row back.

# Write latency: one tree walk per write

A write that cites code references could scan your source tree once per
reference. It does not: one recursive walk, shared by GATE-1 and GATE-2, prunes
`node_modules` and VCS directories, and reads each source file at most once. The
table below is the difference between "walk the tree" and "walk it five times".

**Bench** — measured on a 5,300-file fixture (300 sources + 5,000 `node_modules`
decoys), scope seeded with 5 embedded call forms:

| Call forms in the write | Shipped | One scan per form |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| 1 | 17ms | 105ms |
| 3 | 15ms | 136ms |
| 5 | 20ms | 169ms |

The shipped column is flat: the tree is walked once no matter how many references
the write cites.

```sh
bun run bench:write
```

What each gate does with what the walk finds:
[docs/internals/write-gates.md](write-gates.md).

# Research flags

The three flags that encode a measured finding rather than a preference:
what each one enforces, the evidence behind it, and what an invalid value
does. These are not the general option surface — every other knob lives in
[Options and environment variables](options.md). The README names the three
and points here; this file is the whole behaviour.

`OPENCODE_MEMORY_SYMPTOM` is the clearest case. A lesson saved as "in this
session we fixed the flaky test" shares no words with the query a future
session types, so it gets filed and never found: measured, 0 of 8 diary-shaped
rows surfaced, against ranks 1–7 when the same lesson opens with the symptom.
The flag therefore refuses the diary form at the write gate instead of storing
something unrecoverable.

## Flag behaviour

| Variable | Full behaviour |
| --- | --- |
| `OPENCODE_MEMORY_DEDUP` | Near-duplicate suppression inside a `memory_recall` window. **ON by default at `0.8`** (content-token Jaccard): a row that is a near-copy (same scope, Jaccard at or above the threshold) of a row already returned is skipped — the newest copy of a clash survives — so the window fills with distinct facts instead of repeats of the top hit. Rows that disagree on a negation word, or carry too little comparable content, are never suppressed. Set `0` for the plain top-`limit` slice, byte-identical to the old behavior; an explicit value below `0.5` or above `1`, or one that is not a number, is a misconfiguration and turns the pass off; see [#409](https://github.com/abogartz/opencode-self-improvement/issues/409). |
| `OPENCODE_MEMORY_SYMPTOM` | Enforces the capture convention (#419): `learning` and `blocker` rows must open their content with the observable trigger a future session will hit, as `"When <symptom>: <fact>"`. A diary-shaped lesson ("In this session we fixed...") shares no words with the query the future session types — measured: surfaced 0/8 as diary, ranks 1-7 symptom-first — so the write gate blocks it with a rephrase hint instead of storing something that can never be recalled. ON by default; set `off` (or `0`/`false`) for automation holding a pre-convention backlog. A rewrite that keeps the supersede target's content byte-identical (a metadata-only `memory_update`, retag repair) is exempt — the rule shapes new lesson prose, not legacy-row maintenance. Other types (`context`, `decision`, `pattern`, `preference`) are unaffected. `scripts/symptom-fixer.ts` repairs old rows offline, grounding each symptom in the store's own query ledger. |
| `OPENCODE_MEMORY_QUERY_GATE` | **ON by default**: a `memory_recall` match must share **two** whole words of the query once the query has three content words — except when a complete query term matches an authored keyword unique among the visible candidates after scope and type filters. Automatic injection keeps its two-concept requirement. Set `off` (also `0`, `no`, `n`, `false`, or any zero) to restore the matcher's permissive one-word admission. |

This file holds the other ways to install, how updates are resolved, and what to


```json
{ "plugins": ["/full/path/to/opencode-self-improvement/index.ts"] }
```

Then `git pull` and restart opencode to update.

## Dropping it into the plugins directory

Loose discovery reads `<config>/plugins/<name>/index.ts` and a sibling `tui.ts`,
and the repository root carries both shims for exactly that route. Discovery
copies nothing and installs nothing, so the directory needs its own dependencies:

```sh
cd "<config>/plugins/opencode-self-improvement" && bun install
```

Without them the plugin fails to load, and the host reports it as `Plugin must
export a default definition with an id and an effect or setup function` — the
missing `zod` is the cause, not the export
([#464](https://github.com/abogartz/opencode-self-improvement/issues/464)). To see
which package could not be resolved, run the plugin once from a terminal inside the
affected project:

```sh
opencode run --standalone --print-logs "diagnostic"
```

`run` needs a message: without one it stops with `You must provide a message`
before loading any plugin. The desktop plugin panel lists the plugin and says
nothing about the dependency. The package route above avoids the step entirely.

## Restart rules by host

A config edit needs a restart to take effect. On the desktop app, relaunching the
app is not enough: the background service stays alive with the options it already
parsed, so use `opencode service restart`. That is also why `memory_evidence` can
report a `capture=` value your config no longer contains. See
[docs/reference/troubleshooting.md](troubleshooting.md).

# Options and environment variables

Every knob, in one place — the general option surface. The three flags that
encode a measured finding rather than a preference are documented separately
in [Research flags](flags.md). The README keeps the ones you are likely to
set; this file is the complete reference, including what an invalid value
does.

## Plugin options

Set them in the object form of the plugin entry in `opencode.json(c)`:

```json
{
  "plugins": [{ "package": "opencode-self-improvement", "options": { "injectBudget": 1200, "frontierBudget": 3600 } }]
}
```

| Option | Default | What it does |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `injectBudget` | `1200` | Character cap on the injected relevance block and each contextual pull; trimmed at whole-memory boundaries. Env fallback: `OPENCODE_MEMORY_INJECT_BUDGET`. |
| `frontierBudget` | `3 × injectBudget` | Character cap on the session-start open-threads block. A thread longer than the budget is not injected and is reported as omitted. Env fallback: `OPENCODE_MEMORY_FRONTIER_BUDGET`. |
| `contradictionSurface` | `true` | Experimental: compare guided constant claims with bounded source reads and render a class-specific CONFLICT verdict. Set `false` to skip code checks and retain plain guidance. See [docs/internals/contradiction-authority.md](../internals/contradiction-authority.md). |
| `notifyBlocked` | `true` | Terminal (TUI) only: toast when a write gate blocks a write. Blocks are always in `memory_evidence` either way. |
| `autoCapture` | `true` | Master switch for auto-capture. On, so a plain install mines turn ends and compactions. Set `false` for no capture model call at all. |
| `captureModel` | inherits | `"provider/id"` model used for auto-capture. Unset means the model the session is using, else the host default. An explicit value that is not `provider/id` disables capture with a startup warning rather than substituting a model. |
| `captureMax` | `3` | Maximum candidates proposed per capture pass. |
| `captureOnCompact` | `true` | When auto-capture is armed, also mine the transcript at compaction, before the summarizer replaces it. Its 5-minute cooldown is separate from the turn-end one, so the two triggers' hit-rates stay measurable. Setting it while `autoCapture` is `false` does nothing and reports `switch_mismatch` on the `plugin_load` line. |
| `captureGuidedRules` | `false` | POC: deterministic guided-candidate pre-pass. The user's own lines decide which stated values or rules are guided (numbers, rates, currency, explicit rule assertions) and attach the verbatim quote; the capture model may phrase such a row but cannot clear the flag or the quote, and a guided quote the user never wrote is refused at the write boundary instead of silently stripped. Fires alongside the model pass only — no extra model calls. |
| `pullOutputChars` | `512` | How many characters of a tool's own **output** join the contextual pull's query, after its arguments. `0` searches the arguments only. This is how a fact keyed to something the model only just discovered — an error string, a symbol in a file body — can reach a seat that never calls `memory_recall`. A value that is not a non-negative number falls back to `512` and says so on the console. See the measurement below. |
| `pullTools` | `["grep", "glob", "read"]` | Which tool results may carry a pull at all. `[]` — an empty list, typed on purpose — turns the channel off: no tool result carries a pull. A value that is not a list, or a list holding no tool name, is read as a typo and falls back to the default rather than to no pull, with a console warning either way. |

### What the contextual pull searches, and what it costs

The pull is the one delivery channel that needs no cooperation from the model: it
appends a short block to a tool result the seat is about to read anyway. That makes
it the right channel for a model that never calls the plugin's tools, and the wrong
place to be careless — a wrong pull is paid for by every later turn, and unlike the
injected block it does not ride the prompt cache.

`bench/runners/pull-precision.ts` measures the scope on the committed recall dataset
(355 tool calls per store, stores of 52/200/800, plus random and store-order negative
controls). At store 200, `R@1`/`R@3` are split by whether the gold row was reachable
from the tool's arguments, and `noise%` is the share of no-gold calls that pulled
anything at all:

| Scope | R@1 args | R@3 args | R@1 output-only | noise% on ordinary traffic | bytes/call |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| arguments only | 98.6 | 100 | 0 | 65 | 122 |
| arguments + output, no merge | 92.9 | 94.3 | 18.8 | 0 | 216 |
| **shipped: arguments + output, argument matches take the slots first** | 98.6 | 100 | 18.8 | 65 | 252 |
| the same, with `shell` in scope | 98.6 | 100 | 37.6 | 100 | 389 |

Two things that doc comment would hide. The merge is load-bearing: a combined query is
longer, and a longer query raises the two-concept threshold, so searching
`table_manager.save grep results` on its own drops the row the model's own words matched
exactly. And `shell` doubles the reach while bolting a block onto every plain command —
it is excluded by measurement, not taste. Both arms stay in the bench so the next reader
has the numbers rather than a prohibition.

*First*, and not *last*, is the whole difference in the merge. Three rows is everything a
pull delivers, so merging the arguments-only search behind the combined one recovers a row
only when the output matches nothing: a grep for `table_manager.save` whose output names
three other memories leaves the exact match past the cap. The shipped scope's own bench
cannot see that — both orders score byte-identical at stores 200 and 800, because no
fixture call pairs a precise argument with three output-matching rows — so the case is
pinned by `test/inject/pull-scope.test.ts`. The `shell` row above is where the ordering
does show: taking slots first costs that arm 7.7 points of output-only R@1 (45.3 → 37.6),
because there the arguments usually fill all three slots. The trade is stated in
`src/inject/pull.ts`: intent outranks output, and the price is reach on the calls where
the arguments already match three rows.

Read the no-merge row's `noise% 0` carefully: it is not precision, it is silence. On
every arg-visible call it misses, it pulls nothing at all (the bench's `miss-abstain%`
column reads 100 for that arm), so it spends 5.7 points of recall the model was already
getting to buy reach it could have had for free.

## Environment variables

| Variable | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| `OPENCODE_MEMORY_DIR` | Store location (default `~/.config/opencode/memory`). |
| `OPENCODE_MEMORY_ALLOW_OUTSIDE_PATHS` | Operator-only. When truthy, `memory_export`/`memory_import` accept paths anywhere on disk instead of confining themselves to the store. Off by default. It is read from the plugin process's own environment, so a model cannot grant it to itself through a tool argument. See [docs/internals/import-quarantine.md](../internals/import-quarantine.md). |
| `OPENCODE_MEMORY_INJECT_BUDGET` | Fallback for `injectBudget`. |
| `OPENCODE_MEMORY_FRONTIER_BUDGET` | Fallback for `frontierBudget`. |
| `OPENCODE_COMMANDS_DIR` | Where the plugin mirrors its slash commands (default `~/.config/opencode/commands`). |
| `OPENCODE_VIEWER_HOST` | Interface the editor binds to (default `127.0.0.1`). A non-loopback bind serves the store over plain HTTP with no authentication — only do it on a network you control. |
| `OPENCODE_VIEWER_PORT` | Admin editor port (default `8787`). |
| `OPENCODE_VIEWER_ALLOWED_HOSTS` | Comma-separated hosts beyond loopback. |

`OPENCODE_MEMORY_DEDUP`, `OPENCODE_MEMORY_SYMPTOM` and `OPENCODE_MEMORY_QUERY_GATE` are documented separately in [docs/reference/flags.md](flags.md): they switch behaviour that a measurement decided, so the evidence behind each one matters more than the default.

# Surfaces

Four ways to see the same data. All of them read `memory_status`; none of them
makes a model call.

## Terminal (opencode CLI)

The plugin ships a TUI half (`@opencode/plugin/tui`) that loads automatically.

- **Footer badge** — illustrative `● mem 1157/1200c · cache 96%`: the injected
  block against its budget, plus the measured session prompt-cache hit rate. The
  dot is green (stable and warm), yellow (recent recompute, or 50–90% reads) or
  red (last turn served almost nothing from cache); `—` until the first assistant
  turn, and `—` throughout on a provider that reports no cache usage.
- **`/memory`** — session panel: **CONTEXT** (what is riding the prompt now and
  how much of the budget it uses), **CACHE** (busts this session and the measured
  cache-served share of prompt tokens), **INJECTED BLOCK** (the verbatim block, or
  an explicit abstention), **RECENT BLOCKED WRITES** (with gate reasons), **STORE**
  (active / superseded / open / scopes, plus `malformed` when a row's `ts` is not
  a valid ISO instant — those rows are skipped by every reader). Keys: `r`
  refresh, `f` fullscreen.
- **Block toast** when a write is refused (`notifyBlocked: false` to silence).

## Desktop / web / IDE

The terminal slots do not exist there, so use the self-installed
**`/memory-report`** chat command: the same sections rendered in the conversation.

## Browser editor

`bun memory-view`, then http://127.0.0.1:8787. Bound to loopback; requests are
checked against `Host` and `Origin`, so other hosts must be listed explicitly in
`OPENCODE_VIEWER_ALLOWED_HOSTS`. Listing a non-loopback host serves the store over
plain HTTP with no authentication — only do it on a network you control.
`OPENCODE_VIEWER_HOST` changes the bind interface.

The viewer is a trusted admin seat. Its edits and deleted-entry restores skip the
model-facing grounding and deduplication gates but honor the same value
rejections: [docs/internals/import-quarantine.md](../internals/import-quarantine.md).

# Troubleshooting, full list

The whole list: the problems people actually run into, and the rarer ones. The
README points here rather than repeating the table.

## Rarer problems

| Problem | Fix |
| --- | --- |
| STORE shows `N malformed` | A daily file has a `ts=` that is not a valid ISO instant (typically a hand-edit). Every reader skips those rows; fix the `ts=` or restore the file with `memory_undo`. |
| Stray `*.logfmt.lock` or `*.tmp` in the store | Write bookkeeping left by an older release; safe to delete while nothing is writing. Current releases leave `.store-lock.<file>.sqlite` beside each store file and `.store-batch.<name>.sqlite`: coordination state, holding no rows, one file per lock, safe to delete while nothing is writing. |
| `/repo-init` missing from the command list | The self-install couldn't write to `~/.config/opencode/commands/`. Create it and restart, or ask the model to "init memory for this repo" — the same tool. |
| `memory_init` rejects a call naming `mode` | The code-graph integration was removed (#231) and the tool schema refuses unknown arguments — drop `mode` from the call. Stamps written by older versions (their text carries `graph=`/`mode=`) still read fine; no re-init is forced. |
| `Error: Plugin is not configured` right after `plugin add` | An opencode bug ([#54654](https://github.com/anomalyco/opencode/issues/54654)), not a config problem: the first `plugin list/check/update` against a cold background service reads the plugin inventory before activation finishes. The plugin is installed and loading — just run the command again. |
| Reset all memories | Stop any running opencode session first, then delete `~/.config/opencode/memory/`. On Windows the delete fails with `EBUSY` while a session is live: the store lock is an open SQLite connection, and Windows will not delete a directory that contains one. |

## Common problems

The cases a session actually hits.

| Problem | Fix |
| --- | --- |
| `memory_*` tools not available | The plugin didn't load. Restart opencode and check the `plugins` entry in your config. |
| `Plugin must export a default definition with an id and an effect or setup function` | The export is not what is wrong: the module never evaluated, so the host saw no export at all. A loose copy under `<config>/plugins/<name>/` carries no `node_modules`, and `zod` cannot be resolved from it ([#464](https://github.com/abogartz/opencode-self-improvement/issues/464)). Run `bun install` in that directory, or install the package instead — `opencode plugin add opencode-self-improvement` resolves through `package.json` `exports` and gets its runtime dependencies from the npm plugin cache. The plugin also logs the package it could not resolve and the directory it loaded from, so the host log names the cause instead of the export. Read that log with `opencode run --standalone --print-logs "diagnostic"` — `run` needs a message, and without one it stops with `You must provide a message` before the plugin is loaded. The desktop **Project → Extensions → Plugins** panel names the plugin but does not show the missing package or this fix. |
| `memory_remember` says blocked | A gate rejected the write: a stale code reference, a cited path that doesn't exist in the repo, overlap with a superseded memory, or an ambiguous claim. The reason is in `memory_evidence`; rephrase against current code and retry. |
| `invalid arguments to memory_*` | The call didn't match the tool's input schema; nothing was done and the message names the offending fields. Gate blocks look different (`blocked at GATE (…)`). |
| `memory store is busy` | A store write exhausted its 5s lock-wait budget, so the mutation is refused rather than run unlocked. Retry after contention clears. An operation spanning several files or steps may have completed earlier steps; refusal is not a rollback of those steps. If the reply reports `PARTIAL`, inspect the named rows and `memory_evidence` / `memory_undo` before retrying. A process that is killed releases the lock when it dies — there is no stale window to wait out. |
| Writes report a disk I/O error and the store is on a share | The lock's write-ahead log needs mmap'd shared memory, which SQLite does not support on network filesystems. SMB, NFS and OneDrive-mounted roots are unsupported — move `OPENCODE_MEMORY_DIR` to local disk. |
| Stale plugin after an update | `opencode plugin update opencode-self-improvement` (or bump the pinned `@version` in the `plugins` entry) and restart opencode. On desktop use `opencode service restart`: relaunching the app leaves the background service — and the plugin version and options it already parsed — alive. |
| Not sure which copy of the plugin is running | The `plugin_load` line in `memory_evidence` carries `entry=`, the directory the running plugin was loaded from. A published install names the npm cache; a checkout named in the `plugins` entry names that checkout. Version alone cannot tell them apart — a checkout and the published package built from it share a version, and the npm cache has been known to hold a stale one while the session ran against something else. |
| Auto-capture does nothing | `memory_evidence` says which case you are in from the `plugin_load` line: `capture=on` (the default), `capture=off` (you set `autoCapture: false`), `invalid_model`, `no_capabilities` or `switch_mismatch`. `capture=on` with no `auto_capture_*` line after a session means the pass did not complete, and is not your configuration — see [Auto-capture](../../README.md#auto-capture). On desktop, changing any of these options needs `opencode service restart`. The same `plugin_load` line carries `subscribed=[…]`, listing the event types that subscription really reacts to. |
